script.opening: “The childminder says she won’t have Leo back until these spots have gone because they’re catching. I’m back on shift on Monday and I’ve used all my leave. Can you freeze them off, or give me something that gets rid of them?”

facts.text: Amira with Leo, 4, on her lap, fidgeting and scratching his arm. He rubs his right eye a few times.

About three months. Started on his tummy, now on his inner arms and behind his knees. Small, shiny, skin-coloured bumps, some with a dimple. Some have gone red and scabby where he scratches. Maybe 30 or 40 in total. They don’t hurt.
Known eczema since a baby. Uses an emollient “when I remember”. The skin around the spots is red and itchy, worse at night. No weeping or yellow crusting. No fever.

facts.topic: Only if asked about his eyes or the face
facts.text: One spot on the edge of his right upper eyelid for about a month. That eye has been red and sticky for two weeks. He rubs it. Not light-sensitive, seeing normally as far as she can tell.

Childminder, Mrs Price, told her on Friday: “Not until they’ve gone, they’re contagious, I’ve got a baby here.” Amira works 12-hour shifts as a healthcare assistant; no family nearby; father not involved. Has already had a warning about absence.
Bought an online “molluscum removal kit” (a liquid you dab on). Has not used it yet. Read that freezing works.

Stressed and a bit tearful about work, insistent on removal at first. Accepts leaving the spots alone if she understands why, and if she gets a letter for the childminder. Becomes worried when the eye is mentioned.

ice.ideas: “They’re a contagious skin infection that needs removing, like warts.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: losing her job; she has had an absence warning and has no other childcare. Also guilty that she does not keep up with his eczema creams.
ice.expectations: “Freeze them off or give me a cream that gets rid of them, and a letter for the childminder.”

cues: “I’m on shift on Monday… used all my leave” — the job is at stake.
Leo rubbing his right eye — look at the eyelids and ask about a red eye.
Red, scabby skin around the spots — molluscum dermatitis needing eczema treatment.
“A removal kit” — the risk of irritating eczema-prone skin.

Identifies the lesion on the eyelid margin with two weeks of red, sticky eye as an indication for ophthalmology referral

Explains the natural history (self-limiting, often 6–18 months, sometimes longer) and that treatment to remove lesions is not recommended in a well child because it is painful, can scar and does not shorten the course
Advises against the online removal kit on eczema-prone skin, and treats the surrounding eczema (regular emollient, a topical steroid to inflamed skin; check the SPC/local formulary)

worked.txt: “These are molluscum. They’re a harmless skin virus, very common in young children, especially with eczema. They go by themselves, usually within a year or so, sometimes longer.”
“Freezing or scraping hurts at this age, can leave scars, and doesn’t make the rest go any faster. The kit you bought can sting and inflame eczema skin, so I’d hold off.”
“The red, itchy patches around the spots are eczema reacting to them. If we calm those with a moisturiser every day and a steroid cream on the red bits, he’ll scratch less and spread them less.”
“The national guidance for nurseries and childminders says children with molluscum don’t need to be kept away. I’ll write a letter saying that, with some simple tips.”
“That spot on his eyelid edge, with the eye red and sticky for two weeks, is different. It can irritate the eye, so I’d like the eye specialists to see him.”
“You’re juggling a lot. None of this is because you’ve done anything wrong. Let’s get you back to work on Monday.”

f.learning: Molluscum contagiosum is a common, benign poxvirus infection in children, especially those with atopic eczema. Lesions are small, firm, pearly, dome-shaped papules with a central dimple, often in clusters on the trunk, limbs and flexures. It is self-limiting: individual lesions last weeks, and the infection usually clears within about 6–18 months, sometimes longer. NICE CKS advises that treatment is not routinely recommended in children: physical removal (cryotherapy, curettage) is painful, can scar and does not shorten the course, and topical products can irritate the skin, particularly in eczema. Eczema around lesions (molluscum dermatitis) is common and should be treated with emollients and a topical corticosteroid to inflamed skin (check the SPC/local formulary), which reduces itch, scratching and spread. Inflammation of individual lesions often heralds resolution. Red flags: lesions on the eyelid margin with conjunctivitis need referral to ophthalmology; also consider referral for very extensive lesions, suspected immune deficiency, or uncertainty. UKHSA guidance for education and childcare settings sets no exclusion for molluscum; practical measures are not sharing towels, not scratching or squeezing, and covering lesions for swimming if wished. A letter to the childcare provider is a legitimate, helpful action. Here the real challenge is a single working parent whose job depends on childcare, so acknowledging that pressure and solving the practical problem is central.

points.t: Firm, pearly, dome-shaped papules with a central dimple, often clustered, in flexures and on the trunk. Usually painless [1].
Self-limiting. Most clear within 6–18 months, sometimes longer. Inflamed lesions often mean the immune system is clearing them [1,4].
In well children, cryotherapy and curettage are painful and can scar; topical treatments can irritate. None is routinely recommended [1].
Eczema around lesions is common. Treat with regular emollients and a topical corticosteroid to inflamed skin (check the SPC/local formulary) [3,5].
Lesions on the eyelid margin can cause conjunctivitis or keratitis. Refer to ophthalmology if there is associated red eye; urgently if pain, photophobia or reduced vision [1].
Very extensive or atypical lesions, suspected immunosuppression (including HIV), diagnostic uncertainty, or lesions causing significant distress despite explanation.
No exclusion from school, nursery or childminders [2]. Advise not sharing towels or baths, not scratching or squeezing, and covering lesions for swimming if wished.
Yellow crusting, weeping, spreading redness or fever suggest bacterial infection needing assessment.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Clarke. Hello Leo. What’s been happening?

The childminder says she won’t have Leo back until these spots have gone because they’re catching. I’m back on shift on Monday and I’ve used all my leave. Can you freeze them off, or give me something that gets rid of them?
That’s a lot of pressure with Monday so close. Let’s look at the spots, and then I’ll help with the childminder as well. Tell me about them.
Three months. Little shiny bumps, some with a dent in the middle. Tummy first, now his arms and behind his knees. Some have gone red and scabby.
Are they itchy or painful? And how’s his eczema at the moment?
The red bits around them itch, especially at night. I’m not great with his creams, to be honest.
That’s really common, life is busy. Any weeping, yellow crusts, fever, or is he unwell in himself?
No, he’s fine in himself.

Could you show me his arm close to the camera? Yes, those small, pearly bumps with a little dimple are typical. And the red, rough skin around them is eczema reacting to them. Can you bring the camera to his face? Does he have any on his eyelids?
model.why: Remote examination; checks face and eyes

model.text: There’s one on the edge of his eyelid, this one. Actually, that eye’s been red and sticky for a couple of weeks. He keeps rubbing it.
Thank you, that’s important. Does light bother him, or does his eye seem painful, or is he bumping into things?
model.why: Red flags for keratitis or reduced vision

model.text: No, nothing like that.
What do you think the spots are, and what worries you most?
Some sort of contagious warts. And honestly, my job. I’ve had a warning about absence and there’s nobody else to have him.

These are molluscum, a harmless skin virus that lots of young children get, especially with eczema. They go away on their own, usually within a year or so. Freezing or scraping them is painful at his age, can scar, and doesn’t make the rest go faster, so we don’t recommend it.
model.why: Diagnosis; natural history; why no removal

model.text: What about the kit I bought online?

I’d leave it. Those liquids can sting and inflame eczema skin, and that would make him scratch and spread them more. The best thing is calming the eczema: moisturiser every day, and a steroid cream on the red, itchy patches for a short while. I’ll prescribe both.

For the childminder: the national guidance for nurseries and childminders says children with molluscum don’t need to stay away. I’ll write a letter today saying that, and suggesting he has his own towel and the spots are covered if she prefers.
That would be amazing. She listens to doctors.

The eye is the one thing I want to act on. A spot on the eyelid edge can irritate the eye, and his has been red and sticky for two weeks, so I’m referring him to the eye specialists. They may treat that one spot.
model.why: Ophthalmology referral for eyelid lesion with conjunctivitis

model.text: Oh. Is his eye in danger?
It’s very unlikely to harm his sight, but it’s worth them checking. If his eye becomes painful, he doesn’t like light, or his vision seems worse, take him to the eye casualty or A&E the same day.
Can you tell me the plan back?
Leave the spots, no kit. Moisturiser every day, steroid on the red bits. Letter for Mrs Price. Eye referral, and same day if it hurts or he can’t see.
Exactly. Also come back if there’s yellow crusting, spreading redness, fever, or if they’re spreading a lot despite the eczema settling. You’re doing a good job with a lot on your plate.

social.t: Exclusion by a childcare provider can cost a parent their job. A clear letter citing national guidance can resolve it quickly.
Parents juggling shifts often struggle with twice-daily creams. Make the routine simple and realistic.

legal.t: UKHSA guidance for education and childcare settings lists no exclusion for molluscum contagiosum.
Letters for childcare providers should be factual, agreed with the parent and recorded (GMC guidance on writing reports).

professional.t: Declining painful, scarring procedures for a self-limiting condition is good practice, with clear reasons.
Ask to see the face and eyelids in any child with molluscum, especially if they rub an eye.

community.t: Pharmacists can advise on emollients and explain why removal products are not recommended for young children.
Can support eczema care routines and help with childcare-setting queries.
